Deep behind enemy lines during Operation Red Wings, a 4-man Navy SEAL reconnaissance team was surrounded by over 50 Taliban fighters on the steep cliffs of Mount Sorkh Sar.

Knowing it was almost certain death, Lieutenant Murphy made a choice.

He deliberately walked out of cover into the direct line of enemy machine-gun fire to reach an open rock ledge where his satellite phone could get a signal.

November 21, 2010. Marjah, Helmand Province, Afghanistan.

Lance Corporal Kyle Carpenter and his best friend, Lance Corporal Nick Eufrazio, were manning a rooftop machine-gun post when an enemy grenade landed directly next to them behind the sandbags.

In combat, a grenade gives you about three seconds. Most people run.

Kyle Carpenter dove.

Without a second of hesitation, Carpenter lunged forward and threw his body directly onto the live explosive, using his chest and Kevlar to shield Nick from the lethal blast.

The grenade detonated underneath him.

The explosion shattered his jaw, collapsed his lung, took his right eye, broke dozens of bones, and filled his body with shrapnel. When the medevac team loaded him onto the helicopter, he had no pulse. He was pronounced dead on arrival.

But Kyle Carpenter refused to die.

He flatlined three separate times on the operating table, endured over 40 surgeries, and spent two and a half years in the hospital rebuilding his body piece by piece. Both he and his brother Nick survived.

In 2014, he walked into the White House to receive the Medal of Honor, becoming the youngest living recipient in the nation.

He gave his face, his eye, and his youth so his brother could go home to his family.

Semper Fidelis isn't just a motto. It's a promise kept in blood.

The Navajo were honored first, in 2001 — but they were never the only ones. Choctaw and Cherokee soldiers had spoken the first coded words in 1918. Comanche men hit Utah Beach on D-Day. Hopi, Lakota, Pawnee, Creek, Seminole and more — in all, members of more than thirty tribes carried their languages into America's wars, and most of them went to their graves officially unrecognized.

The Code Talkers Recognition Act of 2008 set out to fix that, and on November 20, 2013, in the United States Capitol, it happened: Congressional Gold Medals were presented honoring twenty-five more tribes' code talkers, with silver medals for the individual men and their families. Old soldiers in red caps and yellow scarves — and widows and grandsons standing in for those who never lived to see it — finally heard a grateful nation say their names out loud.

The men in this photograph, Navajo elders in their eighties and nineties, sat for honors that arrived two generations late. Their verdict on the long wait was the same grace they'd shown in 1945: no bitterness, just pride. The medals were gold. The men were better.

For twenty-three years, America's greatest battlefield secret was guarded by the men's own silence. 🇺🇸

When the code talkers came home in 1945, their officers gave them one final order: tell no one. Not their wives, not their children, not anyone — what they had done, and how. The code was still a classified military asset, and so some of America's most remarkable veterans went back to their farms, ranches and oil fields carrying a story they were forbidden to share.

They kept that silence until 1968, when the Pentagon finally declassified the code talker program. Only then — twenty-three years later — could the men explain the strange questions their families had always wondered about. Slowly, the nation began to understand: President Reagan proclaimed a National Navajo Code Talkers Day in 1982; in 2001, the surviving Original 29 received Congressional Gold Medals, and every other Navajo talker the Silver.

The men in this photograph are the elders of that brotherhood in their later years, gathered at their traveling display — the portraits of their fallen friends on the banner behind them — still driving to schools, museums and veterans' events in their nineties to tell the story in person. Every year, there are fewer chairs filled at that table. What they ask of us is simple: remember the code, and remember who spoke it.

This is the full team: the Comanche code talkers of the U.S. Army's 4th Signal Company, 4th Infantry Division — front row, second from right, Charles Chibitty; with him Roderick Red Elk, Simmons Parker, Larry Saupitty, Melvin Permansu, Willie Yackeshi, Wellington Mihecoby, and behind them Morris Sunrise, Perry Noyebad, Ralph Wahnee, Haddon Codynah, Robert Holder, Albert Nahquaddy, Clifford Ototivo and Forrest Tsimpoid, among their brothers of the seventeen.

Recruited from Oklahoma beginning in 1940 and hardened at Fort Benning, Georgia, these men built a Comanche military vocabulary of more than a hundred terms — because their ancient language had no words for things like tanks, bombers or Adolf Hitler, they invented them: Hitler became "Crazy White Man," a tank a "turtle," and a machine gun a "sewing machine." Then they memorized all of it, because in the field, nothing could be written.

On D-Day they hit Utah Beach with the first waves of the 4th Infantry Division and kept the division talking — securely — from Normandy to the heart of Germany. Not one Comanche transmission was ever understood by the enemy. Seventeen men did that. When the Army finally told the story decades later, America learned that one of its most effective secret weapons in Europe had been a language spoken around Comanche campfires for a thousand years.

Charles Joyce Chibitty was a Comanche kid from near Medicine Park, Oklahoma, when the Army came looking for men who spoke his language. He became one of just seventeen Comanche code talkers assigned to the 4th Infantry Division — a tiny band of men carrying an outsized secret into the biggest invasion in history.

On the morning of June 6, 1944, Chibitty came ashore at Utah Beach on D-Day, among the very first code talkers to put the language to work in Europe. From that beachhead across France and into Germany, the Comanche talkers sent their coded messages — tank became "turtle," a bomber a "pregnant airplane," a machine gun a "sewing machine" — and German intelligence, for all its brilliance, never understood a single transmission.

Chibitty fought through the whole campaign and came home to Oklahoma, where in his later years he became the honored elder of the Comanche code talkers — traveling, teaching, and reminding America that Native men had helped win the war in a voice straight from their own grandmothers' kitchens. Honors found him at last, including the Army's Knowlton Award for intelligence work. When Charles Chibitty died on July 20, 2005, the last surviving Comanche code talker went silent — but the seventeen voices of the 4th Signal Company are part of D-Day forever.

The code talkers did not begin in World War II. They began in France, in 1918. 🇺🇸

In October 1918, during the Meuse-Argonne offensive, the American 36th Division had a deadly problem: German listeners tapped their phone lines at will, and every code the Americans tried was broken within hours. Then an officer overheard two of his own soldiers chatting in Choctaw — and realized he was listening to a language no German on Earth could understand.

Within days, Choctaw soldiers of the 141st Infantry were manning field telephones across the sector, relaying orders for troop movements and artillery in their native tongue. The Germans were stunned into silence. Within twenty-four hours the tide in the sector turned; within seventy-two, the surprised enemy was in full retreat — and American officers were writing reports calling the Choctaw telephone squad one of the cleverest moves of the war.

Nineteen Choctaw men are remembered as the first code talkers — the pioneers whose idea the Navajo, Comanche and two dozen other tribes would carry into the next war. Yet when they came home, their story was buried for decades; most Americans never learned their names in their lifetimes. It took until 2008 for Congress to formally honor them, and 2013 for their gold medals to be struck. This photograph is where the whole legend starts: a group of young Choctaw soldiers, an American flag, and a language that saved lives.

They look like any three young Marines on a troopship in 1945, grinning for the camera with their rifles and gear. In fact, these Navajo code talkers were sailing toward Okinawa — the last and largest battle of the Pacific war — carrying in their heads a code that had frustrated Japan's best intelligence officers for three straight years.

By 1945, more than 400 Navajo code talkers served across the Marine Corps' Pacific divisions. At Okinawa they did what they had done at Guadalcanal, at Tarawa, at Iwo Jima: they turned shouted battlefield chaos into fast, flawless messages the enemy could not read. Everything rode on their voices — artillery fire, casualty calls, ammunition requests, the movements of thousands of men.

None of it was written down. The entire code — hundreds of terms, a full alphabet — existed only in the memory of young men like these three, most of them barely out of their teens, many of whom had been punished in government schools for speaking the very language that now made them irreplaceable. The irony was not lost on them. It was their quiet revenge, and their gift.

Look at those smiles. They knew what they were carrying. Japan never did.

In November 1943, the 2nd Marine Division stormed Betio Island at Tarawa in one of the bloodiest battles in Marine Corps history — more than a thousand Marines lost in just seventy-six hours. In the middle of that chaos, crouched in the rubble with a field telephone pressed to his ear, sat a Navajo code talker, passing the words that kept the battle connected.

Radios failed at Tarawa. Wires were cut, sets drowned in the lagoon, headquarters lost contact with men pinned at the seawall. What could not fail was the code talkers' network: a human chain of voices speaking a language that no amount of enemy listening could unlock. Through them, commanders called down naval gunfire, redirected reserves, and learned where their men still held on.

The young Marine in this photograph has no famous name attached to his picture — and that is exactly the point. The code talkers were not celebrities. They were teenage radiomen who carried the battle's nervous system in their own mouths, island after island, while the world knew nothing about them. Tarawa was their proving ground under the worst conditions imaginable — and the code came through without a single broken message.

Peter MacDonald was born in 1928 in Teecnospos, Arizona, raised in a hogan, speaking Navajo — and when he heard the Marines were looking for code talkers, the fifteen-year-old lied about his age and enlisted in 1944. He mastered the secret code, shipped out with the 1st Marine Division, and served in North China as the war ended, one of the youngest men ever to carry America's most guarded battlefield secret in his memory.

Coming home, MacDonald did something just as remarkable: he got an education. He became an electrical engineer — one of the first Navajo engineers in the country — and worked on advanced missile programs before returning to serve his people. In 1970 the Navajo Nation elected him its Chairman, and he would win four terms, the longest-serving leader in the Nation's modern history — a code talker who had defended his country now fighting for his tribe's water, land and future.

Today, in his late nineties, Peter MacDonald remains one of the last living links to the Original Era of the code talkers — a national spokesman who still travels to tell young people what a handful of Navajo voices did in the Pacific. From a fifteen-year-old who lied to serve, to the leader of a nation: his whole life has been one long act of duty.

Before there were hundreds, there were twenty-nine. 🇺🇸

In May 1942, twenty-nine young Navajo men — shepherds, students, farmers' sons — walked into Marine boot camp as the first all-Navajo platoon in Corps history. At Camp Elliott in San Diego, they were locked into classrooms with a top-secret order: invent an unbreakable code, from scratch, in their own language.

Working day and night, the 29 built it in layers — a phonetic alphabet (A for "ant," B for "bear") and a dictionary of military terms that grew past 400 words, every one of them memorized, because nothing could ever be written down in the field. In testing, they encoded, sent and decoded a three-line message in twenty seconds. The Marines' best machines took thirty minutes.

Their code went to war across the Pacific and was never broken — the only oral code in modern military history that never fell. By 1945 more than 400 Navajo code talkers were serving, and at Iwo Jima their six networks handled more than 800 messages in the first two days without a single error. Their commanding signal officer said it plainly: "Were it not for the Navajos, the Marines would never have taken Iwo Jima."

In 2001, the surviving members of the Original 29 received the Congressional Gold Medal. The bronze talker on his knees at Window Rock, radio in hand, stands for all of them — twenty-nine young men who turned the language of home into a shield for a nation.

Chester Nez was a shy teenager from the Navajo Nation when Marine recruiters came looking for men who spoke his language in the spring of 1942. He became one of the Original 29 — the first platoon of Navajo code talkers — the men handed an impossible job: build a battle code out of a language that had almost no written form, and build it in weeks.

They did it. An alphabet. Hundreds of memorized words — "iron fish" for submarine, "hummingbird" for a fighter plane, "turtle" for a tank. Nez then carried that code into some of the fiercest fighting of the Pacific war — Guadalcanal, Bougainville, Guam, Peleliu — sending and receiving orders under fire that Japanese codebreakers could hear perfectly and never once understand.

He came home carrying memories that haunted him for years, and Navajo healing ceremonies helped put the young Marine back in balance. Through it all he said nothing — the code stayed classified until 1968. In 2001 he stood in the Capitol Rotunda as the President placed the Congressional Gold Medal around the original talkers' necks. His memoir, "Code Talker," told the story at last, and when Chester Nez died on June 4, 2014, at 93, the last of the legendary 29 went with him — but the code they built remains unbroken forever.

“DON’T WASTE YOUR TIME ON ME. I AM IN THE EXPECTANT CATEGORY. I’M DONE HERE.” — Green Beret Warrant Officer Nick Lavery on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In one of the most unforgettable moments on The Shawn Ryan Show, Special Forces Warrant Officer Nick "The Machine" Lavery recounted the insider attack in Afghanistan where he threw himself in front of a rookie soldier to absorb point-blank machine gun fire.

In his own words:

“I snap my head around and see what’s happening. A gunner 15 feet away from the group ripping into the crowd with a PKM. Guys are dropping. Chaos.

My training tells me: move to cover, eliminate the threat. But six feet in front of me is one of our infantry uplift soldiers—young kid, first deployment, fresh out of basic. He’s 15 feet in front of a guy shooting a machine gun in his general direction, frozen like a deer in the headlights.

Seeing that prompted me to move towards him rather than to cover. I put myself in between him and the shooter, back to the gun. I hit him with such velocity that when we made contact, I took a round to the back of my leg.

I fall chest to chest on top of him. A PKM from 15 feet feels like a sledgehammer smashing into your body. Then boom, boom, boom a couple more impacts.

I check the kid. He’s in shock, pale, but no holes in his body. He’s breathing.

So now let’s see what’s going on with me. I rip open what’s left of my pant leg. My right leg is just f**king mangled—hanging meat, tissue, and exposed bone. I am hissing blood out of my thigh. There is a river flowing from where I was struck. My femoral artery is severed. I have maybe eight or nine minutes before I bleed out completely.

One of my teammates gets over to me. The look on his face said everything: Nick’s not going to make it.

I looked at him and said, ‘Listen man, go work on someone you can save. I am in the expectant category here in triage. Don’t waste your time, precious seconds, and resources on me, because I’m done here.’”

His teammates refused to quit on him. They cranked tourniquets onto his mangled leg, stabilized him under fire, and got him on a medevac bird.

Not only did Nick survive having his leg amputated above the knee, but he also refused medical retirement. He underwent grueling rehab, relearned how to shoot, sprint, and clear rooms on a carbon-fiber prosthetic, and became the first active-duty Green Beret in history to return to combat as an above-the-knee amputee.

Ordering your brothers to leave you behind to save others while you bleed out from a severed femoral artery is the ultimate definition of selfless service.

This rare look shows an Uruguayan military member holding an iconic, combat-proven M1A1 Thompson submachine gun—a weapon that first saw action on the battlefields of World War II over 80 years ago.   

Originally acquired through mid-20th-century U.S. military aid programs, the heavy, milled-steel M1A1 Thompson served as a frontline submachine gun in Uruguay until the mid-1980s, when it was officially replaced by the 9mm Argentine-made FMK-3 submachine gun. 

Rather than melting down or destroying obsolete small arms when new rifles arrive, the Uruguayan military has historically maintained a policy of preserving older weapons in deep-storage armories. Because of this, classic firearms like the M1A1 Thompson, M1 Garand, and M1 Carbine occasionally resurface for specialized familiarity training, reserve exercises, or ceremonial duties. 

Weighing in at roughly 10 pounds unloaded and firing the hard-hitting .45 ACP cartridge at 700+ rounds per minute, the simplified wartime M1A1 design is practically indestructible—proving that good steel and timeless engineering never truly go out of style.

On April 7, 2003, during the fierce opening days of Operation Iraqi Freedom, U.S. Air Force Captain (later Colonel) Kim "Killer Chick" Campbell cemented her place in aviation legend when her A-10 Thunderbolt II took a direct hit over downtown Baghdad—and she refused to bail out.   

While diving below cloud cover to deliver close-air support for pinned-down U.S. ground troops near the Tigris River, Campbell had just finished firing her 30mm GAU-8 Avenger cannon and rockets when a surface-to-air missile slammed into the rear of her Warthog. The blast shredded her horizontal stabilizer, punched over 150 shrapnel holes into the fuselage and right engine cowling, and instantly severed both redundant hydraulic systems. 

As the crippled jet rolled violently left and pitched straight toward the streets of central Baghdad, Campbell knew ejecting meant parachuting directly into enemy hands. In a split second, she flipped the switch to manual reversion—a mechanical backup system of pulleys, cranks, and steel cables that pilots compare to steering a heavy truck with the stick stuck in quick-setting cement. 

Escorted by her flight lead, Lt. Col. Richard "Bino" Turner, Campbell muscled the battered Warthog for an hour over 300 miles back to Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait. Rather than ejecting over friendly territory as the flight manual suggests, she elected to land the aircraft with no hydraulic flight controls, no speed brakes, and no normal steering—setting it down so smoothly that the wing's chief of safety remarked she landed it better with no hydraulics than most pilots do with all systems operational. She was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross for her extraordinary airmanship under fire.

A comprehensive U.S. Army medical study examining the brutal physical toll of Ranger School has revealed that female soldiers who complete the course finish in better overall physiological condition than their male counterparts, experiencing significantly less hormonal disruption and preserving a higher percentage of lean muscle mass. 

Conducted by researchers from the U.S. Army Research Institute of Environmental Medicine (USARIEM) and published in the Journal of Applied Physiology and Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, the study tracked male and female candidates through the 61+ days of severe caloric deprivation, minimal sleep, and non-stop physical exertion across the Darby, Mountain, and Swamp phases. 

While male soldiers entered and exited the course with higher absolute strength and power, their bodies experienced a far steeper physiological crash. Men lost significantly more total body mass and lean muscle tissue, whereas female candidates metabolized fat stores more efficiently—preserving their fat-free muscle mass to a much greater extent and exhibiting fewer extreme drops in metabolic and endocrine hormone markers. 

Lead researcher James McClung noted that while both sexes suffered identical declines in sleep quality and physical output metrics over the two-month course, female physiology proved remarkably resilient against prolonged starvation and multi-stressor exhaustion, concluding: "An elite warfighter is an elite warfighter. It doesn't matter what your sex is."

Previously treated as an additional skillset rather than a standalone career path, Marine Scouts now hold their own Primary Military Occupational Specialty (PMOS 0315) alongside riflemen (0311), machine gunners (0331), and mortarmen (0341). 

These specially trained Marines populate a 26-Marine Scout Platoon inside each infantry battalion—as well as scout teams within Light Armored Reconnaissance (LAR) battalions. Each scout team also embeds a certified Joint Fires Observer (JFO) capable of calling in devastating air and artillery strikes on high-value enemy targets. 

Trained in advanced fieldcraft, stealth, unmanned aerial systems, and assured long-range communications, 0315 Scouts are built to slip ahead of the main force, map routes to the objective, and extend an infantry battalion's sensing capabilities across contested littoral and inland environments.

His body and mind were shutting down.

When the uniform came off, the silence was louder than gunfire. Cody found himself stripped of his identity, struggling through neurological fog, and fighting just to function each day.

Through intense neuro-rehabilitation, discipline, and honest self-examination, he rebuilt himself from the inside out.

The scars you can't see are often the hardest to heal.

For the first time since the Korean War, the U.S. Army is actively preparing for the grimmest reality of large-scale combat: digging temporary mass graves directly on the battlefield.

During recent high-intensity readiness exercises at Fort Liberty, North Carolina, combat engineers from the 20th Engineer Brigade, soldiers from the 3rd Corps Sustainment Command, mortuary affairs specialists, and Army chaplains trained with heavy bulldozers and excavators to establish standardized field burial sites.

The metrics from the exercise are chilling:

Standardized burial trenches for 20 fallen soldiers can be excavated in just 75 minutes.

Using eight bulldozers and four military excavators, an engineering unit could temporarily inter the remains of up to 2,400 soldiers within a single 24-hour window.

For the past 20 years in Iraq and Afghanistan, the U.S. military enjoyed complete air dominance. Every fallen warrior was treated with reverent custody and flown directly home to Dover Air Force Base within days.

But Pentagon war games for a potential clash against a near-peer adversary—such as China or Russia—reveal a brutal reality:

Contested airspace, anti-ship missiles, and cyber-disrupted logistics could sever supply lines for weeks.

Immediate air repatriation would be physically impossible, and casualty counts could reach thousands in days.

Frontline units would be forced to temporarily inter fallen soldiers in the dirt to maintain positive identification, prevent disease, and protect remains until the combat zone can be secured for repatriation.

As Sergeant 1st Class Delbert Ruede stated during the drills: "If we went to war tomorrow, we would be making this up as we went along. What we are doing here is taking a scientific, field-tested approach so that we can maintain positive control and respectfully care for our fallen."

Practicing the unthinkable is the starkest sign yet of how seriously military planners view the threat of major war.

Is the military being responsibly realistic about near-peer warfare, or is this a chilling warning of where global tensions are heading?

Soldiers from the Rhodesian Light Infantry practice with their FN FAL rifles on a firing range, around 1977. Known as "The Saints," the RLI was a light infantry commando battalion that built its reputation during the Rhodesian Bush War, and is still often discussed among the most effective counterinsurgency units of its era.

Its fame came from Fireforce, a rapid reaction tactic in which small groups of soldiers were flown into contact by helicopter, often supported by paratroopers dropped from Dakotas, to surround and engage insurgent groups within minutes of them being spotted. At the height of the war, RLI troopers could find themselves deployed into action several times in a short period, and many made combat parachute jumps far more often than soldiers in most modern armies.

The FN FAL was their standard rifle, a reliable 7.62mm battle rifle well suited to the open bush and the close, fast engagements that Fireforce produced.

The Pentagon, U.S. Army Criminal Investigation Division (CID), and U.S. Cyber Command are officially investigating a wave of simultaneous, catastrophic freezer meltdowns across military base commissaries as a suspected foreign cyberattack.

In recent weeks, commercial refrigeration systems at commissaries across multiple major military installations including Fort Huachuca and bases across several states inexplicably malfunctioned at the exact same time. The sudden temperature overrides thawed massive freezer rows, spoiling hundreds of thousands of dollars in groceries and leaving military families with empty shelves.

Federal investigators quickly connected the dots: the incident closely mirrors a sophisticated cyberattack in France that remotely hacked and shut down environmental cooling controls across more than 350 commercial supermarkets.

While spoiled commissary food might sound like an annoyance on the surface, cybersecurity and military intelligence analysts warn that this is a classic asymmetric infrastructure probe:

Operational Technology (OT) Infiltration: Hostile nation-state hacking groups (such as China or Russia) are actively testing their ability to breach the industrial control systems and software running U.S. military installations.

The Wartime Threat: If foreign hackers can remotely shut down cooling systems in base grocery stores, the exact same networked SCADA vulnerabilities can be used during a conflict to overheat classified supercomputer data centers, ruin temperature-sensitive missile propellant in munitions depots, and destroy military medical blood and vaccine banks.

Gray-zone cyber warfare isn't coming in the future—it's already hitting domestic bases inside our own borders.

Is targeting grocery stores and base infrastructure an early warning of a massive cyber conflict, or are military networks too vulnerable to basic commercial hacking?

March 4, 2002. A 10,000-foot freezing mountain peak in eastern Afghanistan: Takur Ghar.

When a Navy SEAL was thrown from a damaged Chinook into an enemy hornets' nest, Air Force Combat Controller John Chapman volunteered to go back onto that mountain to get his brother back.

As soon as their helicopter touched down, they were hit with RPGs and heavy machine-gun fire. Chapman charged uphill alone through thigh-deep snow, assaulted an al-Qaeda bunker, and neutralized the fighters inside.

While assaulting a second bunker, he was shot multiple times and knocked unconscious. Believed to be fallen, his team was forced to break contact down the mountain.

But John Chapman wasn’t dead.

Sixteen years later, declassified high-definition drone footage revealed the truth: Chapman woke up alone on that freezing peak. Severely wounded and surrounded by dozens of enemy fighters, he refused to quit.

For over an hour, he fought a solo one-man stand from a snow bunker.

When an inbound quick-reaction helicopter carrying 18 Army Rangers flew directly into the ambush zone, Chapman knew they would be shredded.

He made his final choice: he stepped out of his bunker into the open, drawing all enemy fire toward himself to protect the landing helicopter until he was mortally wounded.

His solo stand saved the lives of every man on that incoming bird.

In 2018, Master Sergeant John Chapman was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor—the first Air Force special operator to receive it since Vietnam.

This illustration shows the kind of concealed sniper positions the Viet Cong used throughout the Vietnam War. Often called "spider holes," these were small, one man fighting positions dug into the ground, covered with a camouflaged lid made of wood, leaves, and soil, so they blended almost perfectly into the surrounding terrain.

A sniper could wait inside for hours, lift the cover just enough to take a shot, and then disappear again before anyone could locate where the fire had come from. Some positions were connected to tunnel networks, allowing the shooter to move away underground while American troops searched the area above.

For U.S. and allied forces, the threat shaped how they patrolled. Every clearing, trail, and tree line had the potential to hide a shooter who could not be seen until it was too late. It was a simple, low tech solution that proved deadly effective against a far better equipped enemy.

Deep behind enemy lines during Operation Red Wings, a 4-man Navy SEAL reconnaissance team was surrounded by over 50 Taliban fighters on the steep cliffs of Mount Sorkh Sar.

He deliberately walked out of cover into the direct line of enemy machine-gun fire to reach an open rock ledge where his satellite phone could get a signal.

November 21, 2010. Marjah, Helmand Province, Afghanistan.

Lance Corporal Kyle Carpenter and his best friend, Lance Corporal Nick Eufrazio, were manning a rooftop machine-gun post when an enemy grenade landed directly next to them behind the sandbags.

In combat, a grenade gives you about three seconds. Most people run.

Kyle Carpenter dove.

Without a second of hesitation, Carpenter lunged forward and threw his body directly onto the live explosive, using his chest and Kevlar to shield Nick from the lethal blast.

The grenade detonated underneath him.

The explosion shattered his jaw, collapsed his lung, took his right eye, broke dozens of bones, and filled his body with shrapnel. When the medevac team loaded him onto the helicopter, he had no pulse. He was pronounced dead on arrival.

But Kyle Carpenter refused to die.

He flatlined three separate times on the operating table, endured over 40 surgeries, and spent two and a half years in the hospital rebuilding his body piece by piece. Both he and his brother Nick survived.

In 2014, he walked into the White House to receive the Medal of Honor, becoming the youngest living recipient in the nation.

He gave his face, his eye, and his youth so his brother could go home to his family.

Semper Fidelis isn't just a motto. It's a promise kept in blood.

When the code talkers came home in 1945, their officers gave them one final order: tell no one. Not their wives, not their children, not anyone — what they had done, and how. The code was still a classified military asset, and so some of America's most remarkable veterans went back to their farms, ranches and oil fields carrying a story they were forbidden to share.

They kept that silence until 1968, when the Pentagon finally declassified the code talker program. Only then — twenty-three years later — could the men explain the strange questions their families had always wondered about. Slowly, the nation began to understand: President Reagan proclaimed a National Navajo Code Talkers Day in 1982; in 2001, the surviving Original 29 received Congressional Gold Medals, and every other Navajo talker the Silver.

The men in this photograph are the elders of that brotherhood in their later years, gathered at their traveling display — the portraits of their fallen friends on the banner behind them — still driving to schools, museums and veterans' events in their nineties to tell the story in person. This is the full team: the Comanche code talkers of the U.S. Army's 4th Signal Company, 4th Infantry Division — front row, second from right, Charles Chibitty; with him Roderick Red Elk, Simmons Parker, Larry Saupitty, Melvin Permansu, Willie Yackeshi, Wellington Mihecoby, and behind them Morris Sunrise, Perry Noyebad, Ralph Wahnee, Haddon Codynah, Robert Holder, Albert Nahquaddy, Clifford Ototivo and Forrest Tsimpoid, among their brothers of the seventeen.

Recruited from Oklahoma beginning in 1940 and hardened at Fort Benning, Georgia, these men built a Comanche military vocabulary of more than a hundred terms — because their ancient language had no words for things like tanks, bombers or Adolf Hitler, they invented them: Hitler became "Crazy White Man," a tank a "turtle," and a machine gun a "sewing machine." Then they memorized all of it, because in the field, nothing could be written.

On D-Day they hit Utah Beach with the first waves of the 4th Infantry Division and kept the division talking — securely — from Normandy to the heart of Germany. Not one Comanche transmission was ever understood by the enemy. Seventeen men did that. When the Army finally told the story decades later, America learned that one of its most effective secret weapons in Europe had been a language spoken around Comanche campfires for a thousand years.

Charles Joyce Chibitty was a Comanche kid from near Medicine Park, Oklahoma, when the Army came looking for men who spoke his language. He became one of just seventeen Comanche code talkers assigned to the 4th Infantry Division — a tiny band of men carrying an outsized secret into the biggest invasion in history.

On the morning of June 6, 1944, Chibitty came ashore at Utah Beach on D-Day, among the very first code talkers to put the language to work in Europe. From that beachhead across France and into Germany, the Comanche talkers sent their coded messages — tank became "turtle," a bomber a "pregnant airplane," a machine gun a "sewing machine" — and German intelligence, for all its brilliance, never understood a single transmission.

Chibitty fought through the whole campaign and came home to Oklahoma, where in his later years he became the honored elder of the Comanche code talkers — traveling, teaching, and reminding America that Native men had helped win the war in a voice straight from their own grandmothers' kitchens. Honors found him at last, including the Army's Knowlton Award for intelligence work. When Charles Chibitty died on July 20, 2005, the last surviving Comanche code talker went silent — but the seventeen voices of the 4th Signal Company are part of D-Day forever.

The code talkers did not begin in World War II. They began in France, in 1918. 🇺🇸

In October 1918, during the Meuse-Argonne offensive, the American 36th Division had a deadly problem: German listeners tapped their phone lines at will, and every code the Americans tried was broken within hours. Then an officer overheard two of his own soldiers chatting in Choctaw — and realized he was listening to a language no German on Earth could understand.

Within days, Choctaw soldiers of the 141st Infantry were manning field telephones across the sector, relaying orders for troop movements and artillery in their native tongue. The Germans were stunned into silence. Within twenty-four hours the tide in the sector turned; within seventy-two, the surprised enemy was in full retreat — and American officers were writing reports calling the Choctaw telephone squad one of the cleverest moves of the war.

Nineteen Choctaw men are remembered as the first code talkers — the pioneers whose idea the Navajo, Comanche and two dozen other tribes would carry into the next war. Yet when they came home, their story was buried for decades; most Americans never learned their names in their lifetimes. It took until 2008 for Congress to formally honor them, and 2013 for their gold medals to be struck. This photograph is where the whole legend starts: a group of young Choctaw soldiers, an American flag, and a language that saved lives.

Before there were hundreds, there were twenty-nine. 🇺🇸

In May 1942, twenty-nine young Navajo men — shepherds, students, farmers' sons — walked into Marine boot camp as the first all-Navajo platoon in Corps history. At Camp Elliott in San Diego, they were locked into classrooms with a top-secret order: invent an unbreakable code, from scratch, in their own language.

Working day and night, the 29 built it in layers — a phonetic alphabet (A for "ant," B for "bear") and a dictionary of military terms that grew past 400 words, every one of them memorized, because nothing could ever be written down in the field. In testing, they encoded, sent and decoded a three-line message in twenty seconds. The Marines' best machines took thirty minutes.

Their code went to war across the Pacific and was never broken — the only oral code in modern military history that never fell. By 1945 more than 400 Navajo code talkers were serving, and at Iwo Jima their six networks handled more than 800 messages in the first two days without a single error. Their commanding signal officer said it plainly: "Were it not for the Navajos, the Marines would never have taken Iwo Jima."

In 2001, the surviving members of the Original 29 received the Congressional Gold Medal. The bronze talker on his knees at Window Rock, radio in hand, stands for all of them — twenty-nine young men who turned the language of home into a shield for a nation.

Chester Nez was a shy teenager from the Navajo Nation when Marine recruiters came looking for men who spoke his language in the spring of 1942. He became one of the Original 29 — the first platoon of Navajo code talkers — the men handed an impossible job: build a battle code out of a language that had almost no written form, and build it in weeks.

Nez then carried that code into some of the fiercest fighting of the Pacific war — Guadalcanal, Bougainville, Guam, Peleliu — sending and receiving orders under fire that Japanese codebreakers could hear perfectly and never once understand.

He came home carrying memories that haunted him for years, and Navajo healing ceremonies helped put the young Marine back in balance. Through it all he said nothing — the code stayed classified until 1968. In 2001 he stood in the Capitol Rotunda as the President placed the Congressional Gold Medal around the original talkers' necks. When missing by an inch means total mission failure, you build a firing solution out of whatever terrain the mountain gives you.

A Delta Force precision marksman locked behind his rifle system during high-angle mountain sniper training in Hat Creek, Idaho.

This image is a masterclass in modern, non-traditional long-range shooting. In the rugged backcountry, flat shooting benches and prone mats do not exist. Instead, the shooter uses a gnarled tree crook as an improvised front rest, cushioning the chassis on a shooting bag while anchoring his stance on high-elevation carbon-fiber tripod legs.

Look at the hardware mounted to the rifle platform. He is running an advanced precision bolt-action rifle chambered for long-range interdiction, fitted with a high-magnification optic, top-mounted micro red dot for fast target transitions, a dedicated sound suppressor, and electro-optical targeting gear riding the 12 o'clock rail. Behind him sits a secondary heavy tripod rig running an electro-optical spotter setup to call wind and trace across jagged canyon lines.

Operating out of places like the remote Hat Creek training facilities allows Tier 1 snipers to hone cold-bore precision at extreme angles, factoring in brutal mountain updrafts, thin air, and mirage over distances exceeding 1,000 yards.

Low-key civilian outerwear, ball cap, and pure surgical discipline.

Delta Force sniper section. The Unit.

“DON’T WASTE YOUR TIME ON ME. I AM IN THE EXPECTANT CATEGORY. I’M DONE HERE.” — Green Beret Warrant Officer Nick Lavery on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In one of the most unforgettable moments on The Shawn Ryan Show, Special Forces Warrant Officer Nick "The Machine" Lavery recounted the insider attack in Afghanistan where he threw himself in front of a rookie soldier to absorb point-blank machine gun fire.

In his own words:

“I snap my head around and see what’s happening. A gunner 15 feet away from the group ripping into the crowd with a PKM. Guys are dropping. Chaos.

My training tells me: move to cover, eliminate the threat. But six feet in front of me is one of our infantry uplift soldiers—young kid, first deployment, fresh out of basic. He’s 15 feet in front of a guy shooting a machine gun in his general direction, frozen like a deer in the headlights.

Seeing that prompted me to move towards him rather than to cover. I put myself in between him and the shooter, back to the gun. I hit him with such velocity that when we made contact, I took a round to the back of my leg.

I fall chest to chest on top of him. A PKM from 15 feet feels like a sledgehammer smashing into your body. Then boom, boom, boom a couple more impacts.

I check the kid. He’s in shock, pale, but no holes in his body. He’s breathing.

So now let’s see what’s going on with me. I rip open what’s left of my pant leg. My right leg is just f**king mangled—hanging meat, tissue, and exposed bone. I am hissing blood out of my thigh. There is a river flowing from where I was struck. My femoral artery is severed. I have maybe eight or nine minutes before I bleed out completely.

One of my teammates gets over to me. The look on his face said everything: Nick’s not going to make it.

I looked at him and said, ‘Listen man, go work on someone you can save. I am in the expectant category here in triage. Don’t waste your time, precious seconds, and resources on me, because I’m done here.’”

His teammates refused to quit on him. They cranked tourniquets onto his mangled leg, stabilized him under fire, and got him on a medevac bird.

Not only did Nick survive having his leg amputated above the knee, but he also refused medical retirement. He underwent grueling rehab, relearned how to shoot, sprint, and clear rooms on a carbon-fiber prosthetic, and became the first active-duty Green Beret in history to return to combat as an above-the-knee amputee.

Ordering your brothers to leave you behind to save others while you bleed out from a severed femoral artery is the ultimate definition of selfless service.

Drop a salute in the comments for Nick "The Machine" Lavery.

REST IN PEACE: The U.S. Army has identified the soldier tragically killed during a training exercise at Fort Lee as 23-year-old Private Nicholas Chavira.

Army officials confirmed that Private Chavira lost his life during an on-post military training exercise in Prince George County, Virginia, according to reporting from WTVR CBS 6 and Hoodline.

What officials have confirmed:

Private Chavira died during active military training operations in a designated training area on post.

 Military officials stated that no foul play is suspected, and the Army has launched an official investigation into the exact circumstances surrounding the fatal incident.

 Every day, young men and women step forward and put their lives on the line in demanding, high-risk training environments across the country to prepare for combat operations downrange.

Losing a young soldier at 23 years old in the line of duty is an absolute heartbreak.

Please take a moment to keep Private Nicholas Chavira’s family, loved ones, and unit in your thoughts and prayers.
Rest Easy

Ukraine reports Russian military personnel losses reached an estimated 49,040 in October—the highest single-month casualty toll of the entire war.

According to official reporting from the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Russian combat personnel losses (killed and severely wounded) in October 2026 surpassed the previous all-time monthly high of 48,670 set in December 2024.

The operational reality behind the numbers:

 That figure represents an average of roughly 1,690 Russian soldiers lost every 24 hours throughout October across intense frontline sectors including Pokrovsk, Kurakhove, Toretsk, and the Kursk salient.

Combat hexacopters and FPV strike teams played a decisive role in driving these numbers. Data tracked by Ukrainian forces indicates drone operations alone accounted for over 27,800 Russian personnel casualties in the first 25 days of the month.

Moscow continues relying on persistent dismounted infantry assaults and mechanized pushes to seize territory across eastern Ukraine before winter freezes the ground and shifts battlefield conditions.

Despite staggering monthly casualties, Russian forces continue pressing forward meter by meter in the Donbas.

At a burn rate of nearly 50,000 personnel per month, how long can Russian offensive momentum realistically hold out before manpower shortages force an operational pause?

“I FKING LOST THE WILL TO LIVE. SO I DID WHAT I DID.” — Cain Velasquez breaks his silence on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In an emotional sit-down interview on The Shawn Ryan Show, former two-time UFC Heavyweight Champion Cain Velasquez opened up about the February 2022 high-speed chase and shooting that completely altered the trajectory of his life.

In his own words:

“My son was in bed and told me things that are happening to him at daycare. So I ask questions about what happened, he tells me, I said ‘how long has this been going on?’  he said ‘a while.’

So I did what we’re supposed to do. Make a report and call the authorities. They book him, he gets out on Friday that same week with no ankle monitor, nothing. He’s out in two days.

Just seeing my son, the trauma coming out, seeing the hurt in him, him breaking down crying. Seeing Michelle [his wife] break down, and not being able to do anything about it.

Now looking at the signs, my son started digressing in his potty training. So he would just wet himself. He was avoiding going to the bathroom.

I lost it. I f**king lost the will to live. Didn’t care about dying or anything. I was in a different place at that moment. So I did what I did.

I went on an 11-mile chase shooting at him.”

After years of legal battles, months spent in solitary confinement, and a prison sentence, Velasquez was released earlier this year to reunite with his family and return to coaching.

When the justice system releases an alleged child abuser back onto the streets in 48 hours with no monitor, what goes through a father's mind?

Did Cain do what any protective father pushed past the brink would do? Drop your take below.

The three-star general fired as the military's top strategist has admitted to leaking classified intelligence on Iran and Ukraine.

In one of the most explosive national security breaches inside the building in decades, Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia the former Director for Strategy, Plans, and Policy on the Joint Staff (J5) admitted to leaking classified military intelligence to the media, according to reporting from Axios and The Washington Post.

The breakdown of the ouster:

As the Joint Staff J5, Sylvia was the U.S. military's lead strategic war planner, responsible for shaping global contingency operations, force posture, and direct combat advice for the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs and the Secretary of Defense.

Sylvia was abruptly relieved of his duties by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth after allegedly failing three consecutive counterintelligence polygraph examinations during an aggressive Pentagon internal leak probe.

 Pentagon officials confirmed that Sylvia subsequently admitted to unauthorized disclosures of classified information regarding sensitive U.S. contingency planning for war with Iran and ongoing military operations in Ukraine.

While junior enlisted service members and NCOs routinely face immediate pretrial confinement, Leavenworth prison sentences, and dishonorable discharges under the UCMJ for mishandling classified documents, senior flag officers have historically been allowed to quietly retire.

A three-star general sitting on the Joint Staff leaking classified war plans to reporters strikes at the very core of military chain of command and national security.

The lone Navy corpsman who sprinted into a burning building to save six coalition soldiers.

On the night of March 12 in northern Iraq, an enemy one-way attack drone detonated roughly 25 meters from the living quarters of Navy Hospital Corpsman 2nd Class (HM2) Jajuan Hernandez.

Serving as the sole U.S. medic at the outpost while attached to the 2nd Marine Raider Battalion (MARSOC), Hernandez grabbed his weapon, body armor, and trauma bag, sprinting directly toward the fire amidst secondary ammunition explosions.

He arrived at a demolished berthing area to find seven critically wounded French coalition soldiers lying in the dark.

Despite severe language barriers, Hernandez directed nearby Marine Raiders to assist with bandaging and hypothermia blankets while personally executing advanced, life-saving battlefield surgical procedures:

Blunt finger thoracostomy and needle decompression (making incisions to vent air pressure around collapsed lungs and the heart).

Administering fresh whole blood intraosseously ("via the bone").

Applying tourniquets and chest seals under active secondary cook-offs.

 Acting Surgeon General of the Navy Rear Adm. Matthew Case credited Hernandez's quick thinking with directly saving the lives of six French soldiers until medical evacuations could arrive.

In late September, Hernandez was officially presented with the Armed Services YMCA's prestigious 2026 Angels of the Battlefield Award in Washington, D.C.

There is no bond on the battlefield quite like the one between Marines and their Doc.

BREAKING IN EUROPE: Chaos erupts in Warsaw as police deploy outside Poland’s top constitutional court amid accusations of an unconstitutional coup.

A major constitutional showdown has paralyzed Poland’s capital tonight. Polish police vans cordoned off the Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw after government-backed judges moved to suspend the court's president, Bogdan Święczkowski, and vice president, triggering claims of an executive power grab.

The escalation forced Polish President Karol Nawrocki to abruptly abort an official diplomatic flight to Senegal mid-air over southern Spain and race back to Warsaw, writing: "In such a moment the president must be in Poland. I am interrupting the flight to Senegal. I am returning."

What is unfolding on the ground:

Tactical police units surrounded the perimeter of the tribunal building on Wiejska Street as crowds gathered and scuffles broke out. Police confirmed multiple detentions after protesters attempted to scale the security fence.

 Opposition leader Jarosław Kaczyński arrived outside the court, denouncing the move as an "illegal coup against the Constitutional Tribunal" orchestrated by Prime Minister Donald Tusk's pro-EU coalition.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk forcefully defended the measures on X, stating: "Restoring the rule of law is our duty. After years of PiS lawlessness, it is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and requires decisive action. There is no other way."

Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek announced criminal applications to strip the tribunal leadership of their judicial immunity, while the ousted court leadership rejected the orders as completely void and unconstitutional.

With the president rushing back to the capital and police holding the perimeter, Poland is facing its deepest constitutional crisis in modern history.

Palm Beach, Florida.

In an unprecedented escalation of executive protection, the U.S. military and Secret Service have deployed mobile surface-to-air missile systems directly outside Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate.

Moored on a floating industrial barge in the Intracoastal Waterway right off the property's perimeter, photos confirm a pair of AN/TWQ-1 Avenger Air Defense Systems:

The Hardware: High-mobility Humvees outfitted with twin missile pods carrying eight ready-to-fire FIM-92 Stinger missiles, backed by a high-rate-of-fire .50-caliber M3P machine gun.

Target Profile: The Avenger platform is engineered specifically for short-range air defense (SHORAD), designed to intercept low-altitude, high-speed threats including low-flying aircraft, cruise missiles, and loitering suicide drones.

Layered Defense: The floating missile battery operates alongside expanded air defense radar coverage tied into NORAD, establishing a hardened dome over the estate and nearby flight corridors.

While surface-to-air missile rings (like NASAMS and Avenger batteries) have quietly guarded the White House and the National Capital Region since 9/11, stationing military anti-aircraft missile platforms on domestic waterways outside a private residence in Florida marks an extraordinary chapter in modern security.

Federal authorities enacted the heightened measures following elevated threat assessments, foreign assassination threats from Iran, and the rising global reality of cheap, asymmetric drone warfare.

The nature of executive protection has changed forever.

Is deploying military anti-aircraft missile systems on domestic waterways a necessary response to modern drone threats, or a sign of how volatile security has become?

Behind closed doors, the Pentagon has delivered a blunt message to European NATO allies: tone down the aggressive public rhetoric on Russia.

According to defense officials and diplomatic sources, U.S. defense leadership has privately urged several European allies—particularly frontline Baltic nations like Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia—to "cool" their public warnings regarding the threat of direct military conflict with Moscow.

The Pentagon’s core concern: uncontrolled escalation.

Avoiding the Cornered Rat Scenario: Washington warned that hyper-aggressive rhetoric from European leaders—declaring that direct war with Russia is inevitable or framing conflict in absolute terms—risks backing the Kremlin into an escalatory corner and removing diplomatic off-ramps.

Strategic Discipline: U.S. defense strategists are pushing for calibrated messaging, arguing that reckless rhetoric from allies who rely on American military backing can trigger accidental miscalculations that spiral into an Article 5 clash.

The quiet pushback exposes a growing rift inside the alliance:

Frontline European Allies argue that sounding the alarm and showing relentless public defiance is the only deterrent Moscow respects, warning that softening rhetoric projects weakness.

Washington Strategists argue that loose talk and public posturing complicate deterrence and increase the danger of sleepwalking into a catastrophic third world war.

When the stakes involve nuclear-armed superpowers, every word matters.

Is the Pentagon right to demand disciplined rhetoric to avoid war, or should European allies speak out forcefully against Russian aggression?

The War Department is officially launching the Chaplain In-Service Procurement Program.

In a major shift for military personnel pipelines, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that the Pentagon is establishing the Chaplain In-Service Procurement Program (CH-ISPP)—creating a dedicated pathway for active-duty enlisted troops to commission as military chaplains.

The announcement follows Hegseth's creation of the Office of Religious Affairs aimed at prioritizing spiritual readiness and troop resilience across the force.

Key details of the new program:

 Geared toward active-duty enlisted service members (with a minimum rank of E-5) who have a calling to military ministry.

 The program provides qualified NCOs with an active-duty commissioning route to complete their Master of Divinity (MDiv), secure ecclesiastical endorsement from their respective faith tradition, and pin on chaplain insignia without sacrificing military family financial stability.

 Proponents emphasize that bringing experienced NCOs who already understand deployment stress, unit culture, and combat hardship into the chaplaincy will bridge the trust gap between junior enlisted troops and staff officers, reinforcing mental health and suicide prevention efforts.

Transitioning seasoned enlisted leaders directly into the chaplain corps brings a unique frontline perspective to military ministry.

Do you think drawing chaplains directly from the enlisted NCO ranks will strengthen unit morale, or should the military keep relying primarily on civilian seminary recruitment?

After serving his country in the United States Marine Corps, Beltran joined the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department (LASD)—kicking off a legendary 32-year career:

Gang Suppression: Working street-level enforcement against violent criminal syndicates across East LA.

From gun battles and cartel stings to sharing the cage with heavyweight champions, Beltran brought the exact same ethos to officiating that he lived in uniform: calm authority, split-second decisiveness, and an uncompromising commitment to protecting human life.

High above the valleys where the hardest fights took place, standing shoulder to shoulder with brothers in arms.   Delta Force A Squadron operator Lee Vampola, pictured on the far left, unfurls the American flag with his assault troop on a windswept ridgeline.   Born in 1985 and taken far too soon in 2024, Vampola belonged to the rarest breed of combat warriors. To earn a spot inside 1st Special Forces Operational Detachment-Delta demands surviving one of the most punishing, mentally exhausting selection courses known to the modern military. Men like Lee chose that fire willingly.   Look at the team dynamic captured in this mountain setting. Full MultiCam combat uniforms, low-profile ball caps, comms headsets rigged for immediate tactical communication, plate carriers, and dialed, suppressed assault carbines held at the ready. There are no theatrical poses or exaggerated stances here. Just a tight team of consummate professionals who lived in the dark, hunted the nation's most dangerous adversaries, and relied entirely on the operator to their left and right.   Operators inside Delta Force carry out hundreds of direct action raids and counter-terror strikes in complete anonymity. They do not seek fame or public applause. Their impact is measured by the missions completed, the lives shielded, and the brotherhood that holds firm long after the gear is packed away.Husband, father, and Tier 1 warrior who stood at the absolute tip of the spear.Lee Vampola.

This historic combat photograph captures former DEVGRU Red Squadron operator Rob O'Neill (bottom left, with blonde hair) administering IV fluids to exhausted U.S. Army Rangers during the intense search, rescue, and recovery operations following Operation Red Wings in the summer of 2005. 

Operating at high elevations in rugged Afghan terrain pushed even elite forces to their absolute physical limits. Severe dehydration, exhaustion, and relentless heat made basic medical maintenance like intravenous saline administration a daily necessity to keep teams combat-effective. 

During the massive manhunt and recovery mission for fallen Navy SEAL LT Michael Murphy and his reconnaissance team, Naval Special Warfare operators, Army Rangers, and support elements worked side-by-side in treacherous conditions to secure the mountains and bring their brothers home. 

Long before historical milestones or public acclaim, operators on the ground faced grueling, unglamorous days on the ridgelines—managing casualties, combat stress, and severe physical depletion under constant threat.

This rare look shows an Uruguayan military member holding an iconic, combat-proven M1A1 Thompson submachine gun—a weapon that first saw action on the battlefields of World War II over 80 years ago.   

Originally acquired through mid-20th-century U.S. military aid programs, the heavy, milled-steel M1A1 Thompson served as a frontline submachine gun in Uruguay until the mid-1980s, when it was officially replaced by the 9mm Argentine-made FMK-3 submachine gun. 

Rather than melting down or destroying obsolete small arms when new rifles arrive, the Uruguayan military has historically maintained a policy of preserving older weapons in deep-storage armories. Because of this, classic firearms like the M1A1 Thompson, M1 Garand, and M1 Carbine occasionally resurface for specialized familiarity training, reserve exercises, or ceremonial duties. 

Weighing in at roughly 10 pounds unloaded and firing the hard-hitting .45 ACP cartridge at 700+ rounds per minute, the simplified wartime M1A1 design is practically indestructible—proving that good steel and timeless engineering never truly go out of style.

CW4 Keith Yoakum, awarded Distinguished Service Cross, posthumous

Citation of Distinguished Service Cross, posthumous

CW4 Keith Yoakum,
Alpha Company, 1st Battalion, 227th Aviation Regiment
1st Air Cavalry Brigade, Multi-National Division (Baghdad)

CW4 Keith Yoakum distinguished himself by gallantry and courage at the risk of his own life above and beyond the call of duty as an AH-64D Longbow Apache Pilot-in Command while providing cover for his wingman on 2 February 2007 during aerial combat against a deliberate helicopter ambush site.

The previous two weeks in the Baghdad area of operations witnessed four separate attacks on coalition aircraft, resulting in the loss of 19 lives and the destruction of one AH-64D Longbow Apache, one UH-60 Blackhawk, and two Department of Defense contracted helicopters. CW4 Yoakum was the first responder to the UH-60 crash site and was intimately familiar with the enemy's helicopter ambush tactics.

CW4 Yoakum was the Pilot-in-Command of the trail aircraft in a flight of two AH-64D Longbow Apache helicopters as they departed on a reconnaissance mission in support of four separate ground brigades on the morning of 2 February 2007. Just when the Apache team began reconnaissance of a test fire area, waves of red tracers and heavy machine gun fire burst into the sky from multiple directions and raked the Apaches. The tracer fire immediately engulfed CW4 Yoakum's aircraft and riddled his fuselage. The enemy had established a deadly kill zone comprised of multiple heavy machine gun and anti-aircraft gun positions. With its interlocking fields of heavy anti-aircraft fire, the enemy ambush site was similar to the earlier ambush site that had downed a UH-60—the same UH-60 that CW4 Yoakum had responded to 13 days earlier, thus familiarizing him with the lethality of the enemy's tactics.

CW4 Yoakum immediately radioed his lead aircraft to maneuver it away from the direction of fire. As the lead aircraft broke hard to the right, the enemy responded, shifting its fire away from CW4 Yoakum's aircraft and toward the lead aircraft. CW4 Yoakum warned the lead helicopter announcing “now you're taking fire!” and the two aircraft broke left to escape the deadly kill zone.

Despite the damage to his aircraft, CW4 Yoakum took personal charge of the team amid the melee of bullets, calmed his lead aircraft, and steered the team out of the kill zone. The team raced to the north to separate from the enemy force and to acquire standoff range to assess the situation. Immediately after their turn to the north, CW4 Yoakum announced that he had “lost utility hydraulics,” a condition that requires the pilot to land the aircraft immediately at the nearest clear landing area. As the senior maintenance test pilot in the company, a prior instructor to other maintenance test pilots, and a Master Army Aviator with almost 5000 flight hours, CW4 Yoakum instantly understood the gravity of his Apache's emergency condition. Furthermore, CW4 Yoakum recognized that the loss of hydraulic pressure prevented him from employing his aircraft's main gun. As a result, he would have to use the aircraft's 2.75 inch rockets from a fixed position, requiring him to skillfully maneuver his crippled aircraft to accurately employ the rockets against the enemy.

The team continued northbound and after approximately two minutes no longer had tracers whipping by their windscreens. Once clear of the immediate threat, CW4 Yoakum had the opportunity to fly his critically damaged aircraft back to the airfield or land in the open desert to conduct an emergency extraction of his crew on his wingman's aircraft. He again announced “we've got no utility hydraulics left.” Still, despite the cockpit warnings and CW4 Yoakum's own recognition of his grave situation, he never considered leaving his wingman and knew this enemy would kill again if left on the battlefield. The enemy had a distinct advantage as a result of their concealed position among the numerous canals and irrigation ditches in the surrounding countryside. Despite the fierce danger inherent in pressing the attack, CW4 Yoakum radioed his wingman that “I can put rockets in” and continued to plan the route back into the withering fire of the enemy's ambush site to destroy the enemy's anti-aircraft positions.

CW4 Yoakum's instructions to his lead aircraft were simple: “you find them, we've got you covered.” CW4 Yoakum knew that his Apache team had a sliver of an opportunity to engage and destroy the enemy before they blended into the Iraqi countryside. The team decided to search the ambush area in a cloverleaf pattern, thereby performing a sweep of the area from all directions until they were able to locate the anti-aircraft guns. Despite his aircraft's crippled condition and the knowledge of the volume of fire that would again rake his aircraft at the ambush site, CW4 Yoakum was determined to cover his wingman as they searched for targets and eliminated the enemy position which was certain to be set up again at a different time and place to destroy coalition aircraft.

Approximately two minutes after the initial ambush had crippled CW4 Yoakum's Apache, the lead aircraft, acting on CW4 Yoakum's instructions, turned south to begin their search for the enemy ambush site. Despite the deteriorating condition of his own aircraft, CW4 Yoakum announced “I'm going to climb up and cover you from high and we're gonna work on rockets.” As he continued losing critical hydraulic pressure, CW4 Yoakum determined that his degraded weapons systems necessitated that he climb to altitude and then dive his damaged aircraft directly at the enemy to provide effective rocket fire. Only by diving from a higher altitude directly toward the enemy position could he provide precise rocket fire for his wingman while focusing his fires solely on the enemy and away from the surrounding villages and homes in the Iraqi countryside. With unmatched skill and extraordinary courage, CW4 Yoakum began his climb to posture his crippled aircraft in a diving position, knowing full well that his climb would give the enemy gunners a clearer line of sight and more time with which to engage his aircraft as he maneuvered back towards the ambush site.

CW4 Yoakum's focus on the destruction of the enemy's anti-aircraft guns caused him to demand as much from his aircraft as he did from himself, but his dying Apache was not able to sustain its altitude. As the Apache team made a second inbound run to the ambush area utilizing their cloverleaf pattern, the lead Apache radioed to CW4 Yoakum to ensure that he was still with them. After transmitting several radio calls and receiving no response, the lead aircraft began a left turn and acquired CW4 Yoakum's aircraft. After flying for almost four minutes in a critical state, CW4 Yoakum's Apache had succumbed to its battle damage and was engulfed in a blazing fire on the ground following a crash that had instantly killed CW4 Yoakum and his copilot.

CW4 Yoakum acted to protect his wingman and destroy an enemy anti-aircraft position designed to produce the continued loss of coalition aircraft. His decision to knowingly risk his life to cover his lead aircraft, despite having the opportunity to land or return to the airfield, put the accomplishment of his mission and the protection of his comrades over his own personal safety. His personal bravery and uncommon valor at the risk of his own life reflects great credit upon himself, the 1st Air Cavalry Brigade, the First Cavalry Division and the Multinational Division-Baghdad, and the United States Army.

On April 7, 2003, during the fierce opening days of Operation Iraqi Freedom, U.S. Air Force Captain (later Colonel) Kim "Killer Chick" Campbell cemented her place in aviation legend when her A-10 Thunderbolt II took a direct hit over downtown Baghdad—and she refused to bail out.   

While diving below cloud cover to deliver close-air support for pinned-down U.S. ground troops near the Tigris River, Campbell had just finished firing her 30mm GAU-8 Avenger cannon and rockets when a surface-to-air missile slammed into the rear of her Warthog. The blast shredded her horizontal stabilizer, punched over 150 shrapnel holes into the fuselage and right engine cowling, and instantly severed both redundant hydraulic systems. 

As the crippled jet rolled violently left and pitched straight toward the streets of central Baghdad, Campbell knew ejecting meant parachuting directly into enemy hands. In a split second, she flipped the switch to manual reversion—a mechanical backup system of pulleys, cranks, and steel cables that pilots compare to steering a heavy truck with the stick stuck in quick-setting cement. 

Escorted by her flight lead, Lt. Col. Richard "Bino" Turner, Campbell muscled the battered Warthog for an hour over 300 miles back to Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait. Rather than ejecting over friendly territory as the flight manual suggests, she elected to land the aircraft with no hydraulic flight controls, no speed brakes, and no normal steering—setting it down so smoothly that the wing's chief of safety remarked she landed it better with no hydraulics than most pilots do with all systems operational. She was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross for her extraordinary airmanship under fire.
That's cold... But smart!

A comprehensive U.S. Army medical study examining the brutal physical toll of Ranger School has revealed that female soldiers who complete the course finish in better overall physiological condition than their male counterparts, experiencing significantly less hormonal disruption and preserving a higher percentage of lean muscle mass. 

Conducted by researchers from the U.S. Army Research Institute of Environmental Medicine (USARIEM) and published in the Journal of Applied Physiology and Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, the study tracked male and female candidates through the 61+ days of severe caloric deprivation, minimal sleep, and non-stop physical exertion across the Darby, Mountain, and Swamp phases. 

While male soldiers entered and exited the course with higher absolute strength and power, their bodies experienced a far steeper physiological crash. Men lost significantly more total body mass and lean muscle tissue, whereas female candidates metabolized fat stores more efficiently—preserving their fat-free muscle mass to a much greater extent and exhibiting fewer extreme drops in metabolic and endocrine hormone markers. 

Lead researcher James McClung noted that while both sexes suffered identical declines in sleep quality and physical output metrics over the two-month course, female physiology proved remarkably resilient against prolonged starvation and multi-stressor exhaustion, concluding: "An elite warfighter is an elite warfighter. It doesn't matter what your sex is."

The U.S. Marine Corps has officially identified the 21-year-old infantryman from Minnesota who was tragically lost at sea during training operations off the coast of Southern California as Lance Corporal Armando Ortiz Canseco.

Can a dedicated 26-Marine Scout Platoon fully replace the legendary Scout Sniper platoons and give infantry commanders the ultimate eyes and ears on the modern battlefield? 

The U.S. Marine Corps’ newest primary infantry career field—the 0315 Marine Scout—is officially in effect, establishing a dedicated reconnaissance and surveillance pipeline on the heels of the Corps' controversial decision to phase out traditional Scout Sniper platoons in 2023.   

Previously treated as an additional skillset rather than a standalone career path, Marine Scouts now hold their own Primary Military Occupational Specialty (PMOS 0315) alongside riflemen (0311), machine gunners (0331), and mortarmen (0341). 

These specially trained Marines populate a 26-Marine Scout Platoon inside each infantry battalion—as well as scout teams within Light Armored Reconnaissance (LAR) battalions. Each scout team also embeds a certified Joint Fires Observer (JFO) capable of calling in devastating air and artillery strikes on high-value enemy targets. 

Trained in advanced fieldcraft, stealth, unmanned aerial systems, and assured long-range communications, 0315 Scouts are built to slip ahead of the main force, map routes to the objective, and extend an infantry battalion's sensing capabilities across contested littoral and inland environments.

Cody Alford lived at the sharp end of the spear. He deployed on multiple combat tours to Iraq and Afghanistan, leading sniper teams, kicking doors, and surviving under relentless enemy fire.

He earned the Bronze Star with Valor. But the battlefield takes a toll that body armor can't stop.

Hundreds of close-range breaching blasts, artillery concussions, and IED shockwaves tore through his brain. By the end of his career, Cody was suffering from severe Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI), neurological breakdown, vestibular failure, and crippling PTSD.

His body and mind were shutting down.

When the uniform came off, the silence was louder than gunfire. Cody found himself stripped of his identity, struggling through neurological fog, and fighting just to function each day.

But instead of surrendering to the spiral, Cody chose to wage a new war—the war for his own mind and life.

Through intense neuro-rehabilitation, discipline, and honest self-examination, he rebuilt himself from the inside out.

He shared his entire journey on The Shawn Ryan Show, giving millions of veterans permission to acknowledge their invisible combat injuries and seek real healing. Today, through his platform We Are The They, he mentors people to break through mental barriers and conquer their internal battles.

The scars you can't see are often the hardest to heal.

True strength isn’t staying unbroken. True strength is picking up the pieces and forging yourself into something stronger.

For the first time since the Korean War, the U.S. Army is actively preparing for the grimmest reality of large-scale combat: digging temporary mass graves directly on the battlefield.

During recent high-intensity readiness exercises at Fort Liberty, North Carolina, combat engineers from the 20th Engineer Brigade, soldiers from the 3rd Corps Sustainment Command, mortuary affairs specialists, and Army chaplains trained with heavy bulldozers and excavators to establish standardized field burial sites.

The metrics from the exercise are chilling:

Standardized burial trenches for 20 fallen soldiers can be excavated in just 75 minutes.

Using eight bulldozers and four military excavators, an engineering unit could temporarily inter the remains of up to 2,400 soldiers within a single 24-hour window.

For the past 20 years in Iraq and Afghanistan, the U.S. military enjoyed complete air dominance. Every fallen warrior was treated with reverent custody and flown directly home to Dover Air Force Base within days.

But Pentagon war games for a potential clash against a near-peer adversary—such as China or Russia—reveal a brutal reality:

Contested airspace, anti-ship missiles, and cyber-disrupted logistics could sever supply lines for weeks.

Immediate air repatriation would be physically impossible, and casualty counts could reach thousands in days.

Frontline units would be forced to temporarily inter fallen soldiers in the dirt to maintain positive identification, prevent disease, and protect remains until the combat zone can be secured for repatriation.

As Sergeant 1st Class Delbert Ruede stated during the drills: "If we went to war tomorrow, we would be making this up as we went along. What we are doing here is taking a scientific, field-tested approach so that we can maintain positive control and respectfully care for our fallen."

Practicing the unthinkable is the starkest sign yet of how seriously military planners view the threat of major war.

Is the military being responsibly realistic about near-peer warfare, or is this a chilling warning of where global tensions are heading?

The Wartime Threat: If foreign hackers can remotely shut down cooling systems in base grocery stores, the exact same networked SCADA vulnerabilities can be used during a conflict to overheat classified supercomputer data centers, ruin temperature-sensitive missile propellant in munitions depots, and destroy military medical blood and vaccine banks.

Gray-zone cyber warfare isn't coming in the future—it's already hitting domestic bases inside our own borders.

Is targeting grocery stores and base infrastructure an early warning of a massive cyber conflict, or are military networks too vulnerable to basic commercial hacking?

March 4, 2002. A 10,000-foot freezing mountain peak in eastern Afghanistan: Takur Ghar.

When a Navy SEAL was thrown from a damaged Chinook into an enemy hornets' nest, Air Force Combat Controller John Chapman volunteered to go back onto that mountain to get his brother back.

As soon as their helicopter touched down, they were hit with RPGs and heavy machine-gun fire. Chapman charged uphill alone through thigh-deep snow, assaulted an al-Qaeda bunker, and neutralized the fighters inside.

While assaulting a second bunker, he was shot multiple times and knocked unconscious. Believed to be fallen, his team was forced to break contact down the mountain.

But John Chapman wasn’t dead.

Sixteen years later, declassified high-definition drone footage revealed the truth: Chapman woke up alone on that freezing peak. Severely wounded and surrounded by dozens of enemy fighters, he refused to quit.

For over an hour, he fought a solo one-man stand from a snow bunker.

When an inbound quick-reaction helicopter carrying 18 Army Rangers flew directly into the ambush zone, Chapman knew they would be shredded.

He made his final choice: he stepped out of his bunker into the open, drawing all enemy fire toward himself to protect the landing helicopter until he was mortally wounded.

His solo stand saved the lives of every man on that incoming bird.

In 2018, Master Sergeant John Chapman was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor—the first Air Force special operator to receive it since Vietnam.

Greater love hath no man than this.
